controls.notes: Depth of the 2.7 µm absorption of OH in Mg-rich clays (phyllosilicates), from the archived Dawn VIR global mosaic (Survey phase, public V2 calibration). The color scale spans this map's own 2nd to 98th percentile, 0.229 to 0.283, with the rainbow core of the Frigeri et al. (2019), Figure 7 bar. The archived values are deeper than that paper's (median 0.255 against its peak near 0.20): the paper used an artifact correction and instrument response (Carrozzo et al. 2016) that were never released, and a different continuum. Scan stripes remain for the same reason. Gray grid: beyond 60° latitude and other unmeasured pixels.

controls.notes: Depth of the 3.1 µm absorption of ammonium (NH4) in clays, reduced here from Dawn VIR calibrated cubes with the continuum of Frigeri et al. (2019): column stripes and spikes removed, each cube brought to 30° phase, each pixel footprint mapped, overlaps averaged and seams blended as ISIS3 noseam does. Survey and HAMO cubes set every cell they saw; LAMO, then Approach cubes fill the rest. The color scale spans this map’s own 2nd to 98th percentile, 0.106 to 0.151, with the rainbow core of the Frigeri et al. (2019), Figure 7 bar. Values run deeper than the paper’s (median 0.121 against its peak near 0.09) because its response correction (Carrozzo et al. 2016) was never released; the pattern ranks close to its map (Spearman 0.89). Gray grid: beyond 60° latitude and the 1.3% no cube saw under 70° incidence and emission.

controls.label: Gravity
controls.qualification: Dawn radial gravity from JPL model CERES18D to degree and order 18, without the hydrostatic J2 and J4 (PDS4 jgdwn_cer18d_accel_0018 1.0; PDS3 DAWN-A-RSS-5-CEGR-V4.0), in mGal on a 482.0 × 445.9 km ellipsoid, 1° cells.

facts.label: What it shows
facts.value: How much harder or weaker Ceres pulls than a smooth body would: radial gravity on a 482 × 446 km ellipsoid near the surface, from degrees 2 to 18 of the field without the J2 and J4 terms the archive calls hydrostatic.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Milligals (mGal): 1 mGal is 0.00001 m/s², and Ceres's mean surface gravity is about 28,400 mGal. Red pulls harder and blue weaker; values beyond ±250 mGal (0.08% of the surface, the floor of Urvara crater) use endpoint colors.

facts.label: How it was made
facts.value: JPL's Dawn gravity team fitted CERES18D to Deep Space Network Doppler and range tracking and optical landmarks from Dawn's approach to the end of its low orbit, February 2015 to September 2016. It is the degree-18 model the archive publishes as maps; the degree-70 model CERES70E (Park et al. 2020) is archived only as coefficients.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: Degree 18 resolves features about 82 km across at the equator; the field is accurate globally to degree 14, about 105 km (Ruesch et al. 2019; Park et al. 2017). Each 1° cell holds the model value at its centre.

controls.label: Gravity
controls.qualification: One-sigma radial gravity error of CERES18D from its covariance to degree 18 (PDS4 jgdwn_cer18d_accerr_0018 1.0), in mGal on a 482.0 × 445.9 km ellipsoid, 1° cells.

facts.label: What it shows
facts.value: The one-sigma uncertainty of the radial gravity map at each place, mapped by JPL from the model's error covariance to degree 18.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Milligals (mGal). Yellow is least certain: the error grows from 17.6 mGal near the equator to 79 mGal at the south pole. Ruesch et al. (2019) quote about 10 mGal at the equator for the previous version, CERES18C.

controls.label: Gravity
controls.qualification: Dawn Bouguer anomaly from JPL model CERES18D, degrees 2 to 18 without the hydrostatic J2 and J4 (PDS4 jgdwn_cer18d_bou_0018 1.0), in mGal on a 482.0 × 445.9 km ellipsoid, 1° cells. The archive does not state the density it used.

facts.label: What it shows
facts.value: Radial gravity minus the pull the shape of Ceres would have at one uniform density. Positive means more mass below than the shape explains. High ground reads negative and the large basins positive, the pattern of compensated topography (Park et al. 2016).

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Milligals (mGal). Red marks extra mass below, blue a deficit; values beyond ±400 mGal (four cells in Urvara crater) use endpoint colors.

controls.label: Gravity
controls.qualification: Dawn geoid from JPL model CERES18D, degrees 2 to 18 (PDS4 jgdwn_cer18d_geoid_0018 1.0), in meters above an ellipsoid of 482.0 km semi-major axis and flattening 0.074896, 1° cells.

facts.label: What it shows
facts.value: Height of the geoid, the surface of equal gravity potential where a global ocean would settle, above JPL's reference ellipsoid (482.0 km equatorial radius, flattening 0.074896).

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Meters. The geoid stands up to 1,454 m above the ellipsoid near the poles and down to 1,067 m below it near the equator, so the equal-potential surface is rounder than the reference ellipsoid.
